name: Tōdai-ji
info: Tōdai-ji, the Eastern Great Temple at Nara in Japan, was founded in 738 and opened in 752 under Emperor Shōmu; it houses the Great Buddha of Vairocana and was the central temple of Nara-period Buddhism.

facts.made: Commissioned by Emperor Shōmu after a run of disasters and epidemics; the monk Gyōki and his pupils gathered donations, and the temple's records say more than 2,600,000 people contributed
facts.form: A Buddhist temple complex built in imitation of Tang dynasty temples; its Great Buddha Hall is 57 metres long, 50 wide and 49 high and holds a bronze Vairocana, 14.98 metres high by the temple's own figures, weighing 500 tonnes
facts.where: In the city of Nara, Japan, as part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara
facts.known: the Great Buddha (Daibutsu) of Vairocana; the Great Buddha Hall; the Nio guardians of the Great South Gate; the Shōsōin storehouse; ordination under the Vinaya; headquarters of the Kegon school

t: Emperor Shōmu ordered the Great Buddha in 743 after smallpox, bad harvests and a rebellion had left Japan unsettled, and made Tōdai-ji the head of the provincial temples.
In the Nara period it was the central administrative temple for the provincial temples and for six Buddhist schools, and all officially licensed monks were ordained there.
The Great Buddha Hall has been rebuilt twice after fire; the present hall, finished in 1709, is a third smaller than its predecessor and was given a steel frame between 1974 and 1980.
dyk: The 752 eye-opening ceremony for the Great Buddha was attended by 10,000 monks and 4,000 dancers, and the project used much of Japan's bronze and relied entirely on imported gold.
ev: Kinshōsen-ji, the forerunner of Tōdai-ji, was established as a gesture of appeasement for the troubled spirit of Prince Motoi
Emperor Shōmu commanded that a very large Buddha image be built, and work began at Shigaraki
The eye-opening ceremony celebrating the completion of the Great Buddha was held
Ganjin, who had reached Japan after six attempts to cross the sea, gave ordination at Tōdai-ji to Empress Kōken, former Emperor Shōmu and others

Minamoto Yoritomo initiated a reconstruction, entrusted to the monk Chogen

A second large-scale restoration, begun in 1974 and using steel framing, was completed

sections.origins:
Tōdai-ji, whose name means Eastern Great Temple, was an attempt to imitate the Chinese temples of the much-admired Tang dynasty. It was founded in 738 and not opened until 752. Its forerunner, Kinshōsen-ji, was established in 728 as a gesture of appeasement for the troubled spirit of Prince Motoi.

The temple grew out of the instability of the Tenpyō era. Japan suffered a series of disasters and epidemics: an alleged coup d'état by Nagaya in 729, a major outbreak of smallpox around 735–737 made worse by several years of poor crops, and a rebellion led by Fujiwara no Hirotsugu in 740. Emperor Shōmu had been forced to move the capital four times. In 741 he issued an edict promoting the construction of provincial temples throughout the nation, and in 743 he commissioned the Daibutsu, the Great Buddha. Kinshōsen-ji, still going by that name, was appointed the provincial temple of Yamato Province and the head of all the provincial temples.

In the Nara period Buddhism was heavily regulated by the state under the Ritsuryō system, through the Sōgō, the Office of Priestly Affairs.
sections.content:
The temple's centrepiece is the Nara Daibutsu, the Great Buddha of Nara, an image of the Buddha Vairocana (Birushana in Japanese). The temple gives its height as 14.98 metres, with a face of 5.33 metres and eyes of 1.02 metres; the shoulders are 28 metres across, 960 curls cover the head, and the statue weighs 500 tonnes. Its golden halo is 27 metres in diameter and carries 16 images, each 2.4 metres tall. X-rays have shown a human tooth, pearls, mirrors, swords and jewels inside the knee, believed to be relics of Emperor Shōmu.

The statue sits in the Great Buddha Hall, the Daibutsuden, whose roof is carried by 48 lacquered cinnabar pillars. The Nandaimon, the Great South Gate, is guarded by two Nio figures, 8.5 metres tall, the open-mouthed Agyo and the closed-mouthed Ungyo, made by the artists Unkei, Kaikei and their workshop. The original complex also had two pagodas, one on the western and one on the eastern side, each said to be 100 metres tall, along with a library, a lecture hall, a refectory and monks' quarters behind the main hall. The Shōsōin was the storehouse and now holds many artefacts of the Tenpyō period. Tōdai-ji is also the Japanese headquarters of the Kegon school of Buddhism.
sections.making:
In 743 Emperor Shōmu issued a law stating that the people should become directly involved in founding new temples, believing that such piety would inspire the Buddha to protect the country from further disaster. Gyōki and his pupils travelled the provinces asking for donations. According to records kept by Tōdai-ji, more than 2,600,000 people helped to build the Great Buddha and its hall, giving rice, wood, metal, cloth or labour, and 350,000 of them worked directly on the statue.

The statue was built through eight castings over three years, the head and neck being cast together as a separate element. Work began at Shigaraki. After multiple fires and earthquakes, construction resumed in Nara in 745, when the name Tōdai-ji first appears on record, and the Buddha was completed in 751. The eye-opening ceremony followed in 752, with 10,000 monks and 4,000 dancers attending; the Indian priest Bodhisena performed the eye-opening for Emperor Shōmu. The project cost Japan greatly: the statue used much of the country's bronze and relied entirely on imported gold. The hall's 48 pillars are 1.5 metres in diameter and 30 metres long, and they carry a blue-tiled roof.
sections.reception:
According to legend, the monk Gyōki went to the Ise Grand Shrine to reconcile Shinto with Buddhism. He spent seven days and nights reciting sutras until the oracle declared that Vairocana Buddha was compatible with worship of the sun goddess Amaterasu.

In the Nara period Tōdai-ji served as the central administrative temple for the provincial temples and for the six Buddhist schools then in Japan: Hossō, Kegon, Jōjitsu, Sanron, Ritsu and Kusha. Letters of the time show that all six had offices there, with administrators, shrines and libraries of their own. Japanese Buddhism still kept the lineage of the Vinaya, the monastic code, and every officially licensed monk had to be ordained under it at Tōdai-ji. In 754 ordination was given by Ganjin, who had reached Japan after twelve years and six attempts to cross the sea from China, to Empress Kōken, the former Emperor Shōmu and others. Kūkai and Saichō were later ordained there too. During Kūkai's administration of the Sōgō, further ceremonies were added, including the Bodhisattva Precepts from the Brahma Net Sutra and the esoteric precepts of Kūkai's new Shingon school, and an Abhiseka Hall for initiating monks of the six Nara schools was in place by 829.
sections.survival:
In 855 the head of the Great Buddha suddenly fell to the ground, and gifts from the pious throughout the empire paid for a new head. The statue was damaged again in 1692 and has been recast several times, including after earthquake damage; its present hands date from the Momoyama period (1568–1615) and its head from the Edo period (1615–1867). The two original pagodas were destroyed by an earthquake. A reconstruction initiated by Minamoto Yoritomo in 1181 and entrusted to the monk Chogen standardised existing buildings and strengthened visible pillars.

The Great Buddha Hall has been rebuilt twice after fire. The present building, finished in 1709, is about 30 per cent smaller than its predecessor, reduced from 11 bays to 7 for lack of funds. By the 19th century its roof and pillars had warped and by the Meiji period it risked collapse. A first large-scale restoration, in 1904–1913, could not wholly repair the roof, so support beams were added. The hall escaped the US air raids of the Second World War. The second large-scale project began in 1974, mobilised 100,000 people, and was completed in 1980; the roof was removed and fixed with steel frames, and the pillars were remodelled with steel and concrete.
sections.legacy:
The temple's role in maintaining authority declined as the centre of power in Japanese Buddhism shifted from Nara to Mount Hiei and the Tendai sect, and as political power moved from the emperor's capital to the shōgun's base at Kamakura after the Genpei war. The Vinaya lineage later died out despite repeated attempts to revive it, so no ordination ceremonies are held at Tōdai-ji now.

The Great Buddha Hall houses a bronze statue of the Buddha Vairocana that is counted the largest in the world, and until 1998 the hall was counted the world's largest wooden building. Tōdai-ji is listed by UNESCO as one of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara, together with seven other sites in the city. The Nio of the Nandaimon were examined and extensively restored by a team of 15 conservators between 1988 and 1993, the first time they had been moved from their niches. The Tōdai-ji Culture Center, with a museum, library and research centre, opened on 10 October 2011. The poet Matsuo Bashō refers to the Great Buddha in a haiku. After the Notre-Dame de Paris fire of 2019, the temple, which has been rebuilt every time it burned, placed a donation box asking visitors to help rebuild the cathedral.

summary: Tōdai-ji, founded in 738 and opened in 752, was Emperor Shōmu's answer to epidemics and unrest: a temple at Nara holding a bronze Vairocana, the Great Buddha, and the centre of Nara-period Buddhism and monastic ordination. Fires, earthquakes and decay led to repeated rebuilding, most recently in 1974–1980.
notes: Reconstruction under Chogen is dated 1181 (Yoritomo's initiative, lead) in one place and 1180 in the Origins section; 1181 used and the 1180 date left out.
The statue is 16 m high in the Architecture section and 14.98 m in the temple's own dimensions; only the temple's figure is given.

The article says the Great Buddha was 'repaired after significant damage in 1692' but gives no further detail; the present hall is dated 1709. The lead also calls 1709 'one of the most significant reconstructions'.
The sentence 'Hall rebuilt twice after fire' is the article's; the dates of those fires are not given.
Start: 738 from the lead (founded 738, opened 752); the article's event list also gives 728 for the forerunner and 743 for the Buddha.

Left out: films, the 1994 music festival, video games, the novella, the Shōsōin and national-treasure lists (empty in the article), the deer, tourism links. The Bashō haiku text is missing from the saved article, so only the reference is given.
